rows.reviewerNote: Read whole: only the key gives what was seen from the window; no option outshines it; comma, two-part, length and overlap no longer single out the key (measure: none left).

changes.before: That he liked the big house he had taken.
changes.after: That he hoped to see them, and had heard they were beautiful.

changes.before: en-plausible-not-stated
changes.after: en-within-span-wrong-element

changes.before: Nothing says he liked the house; taking it makes it sound like something they could have learned.
changes.after: Lines 5 and 6 say Mr Bingley 'had entertained hopes of being admitted to a sight of the young ladies, of whose beauty he had heard much'. That is inside the window, but it is what he hoped and had heard, not what the daughters found out. From the upper window at lines 7 and 8 they learned only that he wore a blue coat and rode a black horse.

rows.reviewerNote: Read whole: only the key matches line 40; no tell on the key after. Pre-existing staff execution on 'Every dance of the evening.' quotes a line-39 fragment that does not answer the stem; worth tidying, not child-facing.

changes.before: Two: one with Miss Bingley and one with Elizabeth.
changes.after: Two: one with Miss Bingley and one with Elizabeth Bennet.

changes.before: One name changed: Elizabeth for Mrs Hurst. The count and the shape of line 40 are kept.
changes.after: One name changed: Elizabeth Bennet for Mrs Hurst. Line 40 has Mr Darcy dance 'once with Mrs. Hurst and once with Miss Bingley'. Elizabeth sits out two dances at line 47, and Mr Darcy turns her down at lines 66 and 67.

rows.reviewerNote: Read whole: only the key keeps 'without opening it'; no tell on the key after.

changes.before: Read it and then put it away again.
changes.after: Opened it and then put it back in his pocket.

changes.before: Lines 35 and 36 say he put it back without opening it, so he does not read it.
changes.after: Lines 35 and 36 say he 'looked at the edge of it and put it back without opening it'. The child keeps the putting back and drops the 'without', so the paper is opened.

rows.reviewerNote: Read whole: only the key names the Friday box; no tell on the key after.

changes.before: Put it in the returns box, because it had a name in it.
changes.after: Put it in the returns box, low down, and pushed it flat.

changes.before: Line 33 says he put it in the Friday box, the one going to the charity collection. The child follows the rule at lines 7 and 8, that named things are returned, which the passage says Reuben did not do here.
changes.after: Line 33 says he put it 'in the Friday box, low down', the box going to the charity collection, and line 34 that he 'pushed it flat'. The child keeps how he did it and changes the box to the returns box, which named things go in at lines 7 and 8 and which the passage says he did not use here.

rows.reviewerNote: Read whole: only the key fits returning a leaver's cardigan; hedge and length tied; no tell on the key after.

changes.before: He wanted to keep the cardigan for himself.
changes.after: He would rather keep the cardigan for himself than give it back.

changes.before: Lines 13 and 14 have him put the cardigan in the returns box, not keep it. The child gives him a wish the passage never states.
changes.after: Lines 13 and 14 have him 'put it in the returns box anyway', not keep it. The child gives him a wish the passage never states, and one his action contradicts.

rows.reviewerNote: Read whole: only the key states the kept-and-broken rule; the stem-echo is gone; no tell on the key.

changes.before: He could not tell whose the jumper was, so he put it in the box.
changes.after: He did not know the jumper was his until Miss Bhatt found the name.

changes.before: Lines 30 to 32 say Reuben knew whose the jumper was before he turned the collar out, from the shape of his mum's capitals. The child gives him the very doubt the passage rules out.
changes.after: Line 31 says Reuben 'knew before he turned the collar out whose it was', from the shape of his mum's capitals. Miss Bhatt only finds the collar at lines 44 and 45, after he has put the jumper in the Friday box knowing it was his. The child gives him the very doubt the passage rules out.

rows.reviewerNote: Read whole: only the key says how he deals with the rule; no tell on the key after.

changes.before: Miss Deller said nobody was to open the net except her.
changes.after: Miss Deller said, on Monday, that nobody but her could open the net.

changes.before: Reuses line 12 and repeats her rather than saying what he does.
changes.after: Reuses line 12, 'Miss Deller did say nobody was to open the net except her. She said it on Monday', and repeats her rather than saying what he does with it. Lines 13 and 14 give that: 'by Thursday the instruction is basically out of date'.

rows.reviewerNote: Read whole: only the key is what he says of Reception (line 26); comma, two-part and length broken; stem overlap was already on the key and is not failing.

changes.before: They had to sit down and have a drink of water.
changes.after: They sit down on the PE bench, and each have a long drink of water.

changes.before: True at line 25, and it belongs to Miss Deller, not Reception.
changes.after: True at line 25 of Miss Deller, who 'sits down on the PE bench and has a long drink of water', carried across to Reception. Line 26 gives what Dilan says of Reception: 'Reception are fine.'

rows.reviewerNote: Read whole: only the key fits both replies (lines 17, 21-22); the new wrong-speaker option fails on the first reply; no tell on the key after. Two options now share the 'Both are about...' frame, which still needs reading to choose.

changes.before: Both show he agrees with Ilya's plans.
changes.after: Both are about Whitby and Ilya's group, not the lockers.

changes.before: en-plausible-not-stated
changes.after: en-within-span-wrong-element

changes.before: Supplies the agreement a friend might be expected to give, which the passage never states. Neither reply mentions the lockers or Whitby: line 17 is about jumper sizes and lines 21 and 22 about a swimming hat, so there is nothing in them to agree with.
changes.after: Whitby and the group are inside the window but belong to the other speaker: they are Ilya's subject at lines 19 and 20. Reuben's two replies are about the sorting: 'These are all size nine' at line 17, and the swimming hat at lines 21 and 22.

rows.reviewerNote: Read whole: only the key gives his behaviour (lines 31-33); no tell on the key after.

changes.before: He complained that the ball had ended too early.
changes.after: He was angry, complaining that the ball had ended far too early.

changes.before: Complaining that the ball closed early is Mr Bingley at line 37, transferred to Mr Darcy. Lines 31 and 32 give what changed the room: his manners, as he was found to be proud and above his company.
changes.after: Line 37 gives this to Mr Bingley, who 'was angry that the ball closed so early', and the child carries it across to Mr Darcy. Lines 31 to 33 give what changed the room: 'his manners gave a disgust', as he was found 'to be proud, to be above his company'.

rows.reviewerNote: Read whole: only the key gives his stated reason (lines 28-29); no tell on the key after.

changes.before: The family would go on feeding him if he stayed.
changes.after: The family would keep on feeding him raw meat if he stayed.

changes.before: A bargain the lines never give him. Lines 28 and 29 give his own reason, that there is more to find out in this house.
changes.after: A bargain the lines never give him. Line 25 says he 'liked it immensely', but lines 28 and 29 give his own reason: 'There are more things to find out about in this house'.

rows.reviewerNote: Read whole: only the key says what the garden means to him (line 44); no tell on the key after.

changes.before: It was large and only half looked after.
changes.after: It was a large garden and only half looked after.

changes.before: Reuses lines 41 and 42 and describes it rather than saying what it means.
changes.after: Reuses lines 41 and 42, 'a large garden, only half cultivated', and describes the garden rather than saying what it means to him. Line 44 gives that: 'This is a splendid hunting-ground'.

rows.reviewerNote: Read whole: only the key names the armed men out of place; 'not' and length tied; no tell on the key after.

changes.before: The little station was too small for so many people.
changes.after: The little station was not big enough for so many people.

changes.before: A likely enough complaint; lines 11 to 16 never say it.
changes.after: A likely enough complaint about a small wayside station, but lines 11 to 16 never say it. Watson's surprise at lines 12 to 14 is at 'two soldierly men in dark uniforms' with rifles in 'a sweet, simple country spot'.

rows.reviewerNote: Read whole: only the key gives the hiss from the grass as the reason; no tell on the key after.

changes.before: Because they had already told him about the baby.
changes.after: Because they had already told him what happened to the baby.

changes.before: True at lines 52 and 53, before the hiss came. The child answers from the earlier talk, but lines 55 and 56 give the hiss from the grass as the reason they say nothing.
changes.after: True at lines 52 and 53, before the hiss came: 'One of our babies fell out of the nest yesterday and Nag ate him.' The child answers from the earlier talk, but lines 55 and 56 give the hiss from the grass as the reason they say nothing.

rows.reviewerNote: Read whole: only the key is behind the countryside (line 19); no tell on the key after.

changes.before: Old gabled houses among the thick green foliage.
changes.after: Old gabled houses, peeping out from the green foliage.

changes.before: True at lines 17 and 18, and it is part of the sunlit country rather than behind it.
changes.after: True at lines 17 and 18, where 'old gabled houses peeped out from amid the thick green foliage', and part of the sunlit country rather than behind it. Line 19 gives what rose behind it: 'the long, gloomy curve of the moor'.

rows.reviewerNote: Read whole: only the key is line 17's reason; overlap and 'not' broken; shortest was already on the key and is not failing.

changes.before: A plan no line gives him.
changes.after: A plan no line gives him. Line 17 gives the reason for the lunchbox, 'The net will not carry flat', and at lines 18 and 19 two more ride openly on his sleeve 'the whole way'.

changes.before: A lunchbox would keep them warm on the way.
changes.after: The governors tell him not to carry the net.

changes.before: A closed box invites warmth; line 18 leaves the lid unclicked.
changes.after: Nothing in lines 17 to 20 has the governors tell him anything. Line 20 says 'Nobody tells me the governors are in the hall', so he does not know they are there. Line 17 gives the reason he uses the lunchbox: 'The net will not carry flat'.

rows.reviewerNote: Read whole: only the key is Mr Okafor's speech; longest broken; no tell on the key after.

changes.before: That two of them are up on the beam.
changes.after: That two of them are up on the beam over the stage where the ropes hang.

changes.before: True at line 29, and it is where they are rather than what he says.
changes.after: True at line 29, 'Two are up on the beam over the stage where the ropes hang', and Dilan's own account of where they are. What Mr Okafor says, at lines 29 and 30, is that 'nobody is going up there for a butterfly, not today'.

rows.reviewerNote: Read whole: only the key fits 'with great spirit' and 'delighted in anything ridiculous'; longest broken; fewest-window-words was already on the key and is not failing.

changes.before: She wants her friends to feel sorry for her.
changes.after: She wants her friends to feel sorry for her after how badly she was treated.

changes.before: A wish for sympathy is supplied; lines 71 and 72 give her a lively, playful disposition instead.
changes.after: A wish for sympathy is supplied. Mr Darcy's slight at lines 66 to 68 is real, but lines 71 to 73 say she told the story 'with great spirit' because she 'delighted in anything ridiculous', which is the opposite of asking for pity.

rows.reviewerNote: Read whole: only the key fits the long look followed by folding it his way; no tell on the key after.

changes.before: She is waiting for him to say sorry for the mistake.
changes.after: She thinks he made a mistake, and waits for him to say sorry.

changes.before: Invents a demand; at line 49 she folds the jumper away as he had it.
changes.after: Invents a demand. At line 47 Reuben gives his reason, 'It won't fit me next year', and at lines 48 and 49 she folds the jumper 'the way he had folded it' and shuts the box, waiting for nothing from him.

rows.reviewerNote: Read whole: only the key is his explanation (line 39); no tell on the key after.

changes.before: His mother came at half past two.
changes.after: His mother arrived at half past two, which is early for her.

changes.before: True at line 36, and it is early for her rather than an explanation.
changes.after: True at line 36, 'She came at half past two, which is early for her', and a fact about his mother rather than his explanation. Line 39 gives that: the word 'again' 'will be about the fountain, and the fountain was ages ago'.

changes.before: A promise the lines never give her.
changes.after: A promise the lines never give her. At lines 36 and 37 she says nothing on the way past, only 'a small nod'. Line 39 gives his own explanation of 'again': 'that will be about the fountain, and the fountain was ages ago'.

rows.reviewerNote: Read whole: 'face, and the look on it' is the only sense that fits both lines 24 and 34; two-part and overlap broken; shortest-characters was already on the key and is not failing.

changes.before: The way a person speaks to other people.
changes.after: A person's manners, and how pleasant they are.

changes.before: en-within-span-wrong-element
changes.after: en-coordination-wrong-conjunct

changes.before: The way a person speaks is lines 24 and 25 — 'easy, unaffected manners'. True, inside the window, and a different quality from the one the word names.
changes.after: Lines 24 and 25 put the word in a pair: 'a pleasant countenance, and easy, unaffected manners'. The child glosses 'countenance' with the other half of the pair, manners, and keeps the 'pleasant' beside it. Lines 31 to 34 keep the two apart for Mr Darcy too: 'his manners gave a disgust' is one fault and his 'disagreeable countenance' another.

rows.reviewerNote: Read whole: only the key fits 'a stranger here' followed by 'Who is Nag?'; comma broken; longest-characters was already on the key and is not failing.

changes.before: Somebody more strange than Darzee.
changes.after: Somebody odd, who is more strange than Darzee.

changes.before: Built from strange plus an ending, which the word looks like.
changes.after: Built from 'strange' plus the ending -er, as if the word meant more strange. At line 54 Rikki-tikki says 'I am a stranger here' and asks who Nag is: he is new to the place, not odd.

rows.reviewerNote: Read whole: only the key gives what the flame did; no tell on the key after. Drafter's note misdescribes the change (no 'Marley's Ghost' in the new value).

changes.before: It called out that it knew Marley.
changes.after: It cried out loud that it knew Marley.

changes.before: Line 70 says as though it cried, so the flame is given a voice it does not have.
changes.after: Lines 69 and 70 say the flame leaped up 'as though it cried, "I know him; Marley's Ghost!"'. The 'as though' makes it a picture of the flame, and the child gives it a real voice.
